headlines.title: San Jose City Council approves municipal garage rate hikes, puts street parking meter increases on hold
headlines.description: Parking in downtown San Jose is about to get more expensive, though not quite as pricey as city leaders originally proposed. The City Council voted Tuesday night to approve higher rates at several municipal garages while putting a controversial plan to raise street parking rates on hold. The garage behind San Pedro Square is among those where drivers will soon pay more. Under the new plan, motorists will still get their first 90 minutes free, but the hourly rate after that will increase by $1. In addition, special event parking rates will rise by $5. The decision follows more than two hours of public comment and debate as downtown businesses continue working to bring customers back. “I just don’t see why I should continue to invest in the city that won’t invest in me,” said Cache Bouren, a local bar owner who opposed the broader rate hikes. Councilmember Anthony Tordillos of District 3, who represents downtown, acknowledged the delicate balance facing local merchants. “I think the big concerns are still about the fact that downtown is still in recovery post-pandemic,” Tordillos said. The council ultimately rejected two other major proposals: raising street meter rates from their current levels and extending meter enforcement until 9 p.m. However, those proposals could return as the city looks for ways to pay for parking garage maintenance and equipment upgrades. “Staff is going to do more analysis to figure out what are the revenue needs to maintain our garages, do equipment upgrades for things like our meters—we need to see how we replenish those funds and make it sustainable,” Tordillos explained. For some residents, the shifting costs are already altering how they visit the city core. “I feel like either way, you’re going to have to pay. There’s no more free parking. You get lucky if you get free parking,” said Ana, a San Jose resident. “It’s always, ‘I have to pay, so let’s just Uber.’ At the end of the day, it’s cheaper.” The council also voted to expand a discounted parking program for eligible downtown employees. As for the street meter increases, they are off the table for now, but city staff will continue studying how to cover the cost of maintaining San Jose’s parking system.

headlines.title: HUD's $4B grant program aims to reduce homelessness, but will it do the opposite?
headlines.description: The federal government is drastically changing the way homeless programs throughout America are funded, but nonprofits and local governments warn the move could put roughly 100,000 people at risk of losing their housing. “This is a population that, by definition, needs stability,” said Tony LoPresti, the top attorney for Santa Clara County, which joined other local governments and nonprofits across the country in filing suit against the federal government seeking to have the new funding restrictions thrown out. “These are new rules that go against decades of evidence that have proven what works when it comes to homelessness prevention.” Tony LoPresti is Santa Clara County’s lead attorney, who is overseeing the county’s lawsuit against HUD that was filed in an effort to block new restrictions on federal funding meant to combat homelessness. New HUD rules favor temporary housing for homeless over long-term programs At issue are major policy changes being implemented by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, which aim to steer federal funding away from homeless programs that offer long-term subsidized housing and instead prioritize initiatives that provide transitional or temporary housing. For communities across the U.S., including in the Bay Area, the changes could result in millions of dollars in funding cuts to individual homelessness programs. “It’s hard to overstate how important this battle is,” LoPresti said. “You’re going to have local governments and other service providers that are going have to make a deeply problematic choice about whether they’re going pull from other pots of funding to sustain a program or cut the program altogether.” HUD’s grant process, known as the Continuum of Care (CoC) Program Competition, is making more than $4 billion available for homelessness programs as part of its 2026 application process. While permanent housing programs have historically received about 90 percent of the funding, HUD is now setting aside $1.3 billion, or about a third of the funding, for new projects prioritizing transitional housing as well as supportive services that don’t include housing, like job training and substance use treatment programs. HUD is also prioritizing housing programs that require participants to engage in certain services, such as job training and substance use treatment, as a condition of receiving federally subsidized housing. Federal govt. is dramatically reshaping homelessness policies The change represents a major shift in U.S. homelessness policy. Beginning with the George W. Bush administration in the early 2000s, the federal government increasingly embraced what became known as a Housing First approach, which focuses on placing people experiencing homelessness into permanent housing without requiring preconditions, such as rehab or mental health services. “I’m worried for myself and I’m also worried there’s going to be more and more people homeless,” said Daniel Hayward, who lives at a federally subsidized housing facility in Oakland that is now at risk of losing funding because of HUD’s new policies. “It’s frustrating – the anxiety, that pressure, it just builds on you.” Hayward spent three years homeless, living in the backseat of his small car, prior to moving into the permanent housing facility, which now provides shelter and supportive services to Hayward and roughly 100 other people. “If you don’t have the permanent housing, you’re just going to move people from one place to another,” Hayward said. “It’s temporary – that’s the whole word, temporary. We need the permanent solution.” Daniel Hayward, who become homeless at 60 years old, is once again in danger of losing his housing in light of HUD’s new funding restrictions that steer money away from long-term housing subsidies, like the one currently funding Hayward’s 100-person apartment building in Oakland. While researchers and homeless advocates have long viewed the Housing First model as a best practice, the Trump administration has characterized it as a “failure,” repeatedly pointing to increased government spending and a rise in homelessness over the past decade. HUD counted 745,652 people experiencing homelessness on a single night in January 2025. Housing alone will not solve a crisis driven by addiction and mental illness. Under President Trump’s leadership, HUD is making necessary reforms to put recovery first. Scott Turner, HUD Secretary “The ‘housing first’ experiment failed Americans by warehousing the vulnerable without results,” HUD Secretary Scott Turner noted in an agency press release back in June announcing the start of this year’s grant process. “Housing alone will not solve a crisis driven by addiction and mental illness. Under President Trump’s leadership, HUD is making necessary reforms to put recovery first.” HUD Secretary Scott Turner has voiced sharp criticism for the federal government’s long-held homeless policy known as Housing First, which prioritizes providing long-term housing to the homeless without requiring preconditions such as rehab or job training. “The ‘housing first’ experiment failed Americans by warehousing the vulnerable without results,” Turner said. HUD’s new funding policies run counter to its own previous research HUD says its approach is intended to address what it describes as the underlying causes of homelessness by directing more funding toward treatment, recovery, job training, and other services designed to promote self-sufficiency. HUD’s criticism of the Housing First model, however, differs sharply from its own previous findings. “The research literature has nearly reached consensus that providing permanent housing—without mandating sobriety, treatment, or service participation to demonstrate housing readiness—is effective in helping people exit homelessness and achieve long-term housing stability,” HUD noted in a 2024 report. In response to the apparent contradiction, a HUD spokesperson told NBC Bay Area “Housing First has failed our most vulnerable and enabled addiction,” adding “the data proves it, and it is shameful the Biden administration doubled down on this failed policy.” Homeless advocates and service providers say temporary housing, including transitional housing facilities, provides a necessary service for people experiencing homelessness, but argue shifting funding away from permanent housing in order to provide more temporary beds will only hurt an already vulnerable population. There’s absolutely nothing wrong with temporary solutions, but absent permanent solutions, they don’t go anywhere. Vivian Wan, CEO of Abode Services “There’s absolutely nothing wrong with temporary solutions, but absent permanent solutions, they don’t go anywhere,” said Vivian Wan, CEO of Abode Services, a nonprofit that provides housing and homelessness services to more than 18,000 people each year in the Bay Area. “People don’t go into shelter and transitional housing and come out of it magically earning $55 an hour, right? That’s really what you have to earn to be able to afford the Bay Area.” Wan fears HUD’s new funding restrictions will lead to a dramatic increase in homelessness. “Absent that money, people can’t pay rent,” she said. “The concern was, is, continues to be, that it’ll push those people out of housing.” Vivian Wan is CEO of Abode Services, a nonprofit that provides housing and homelessness services to about 18,000 each year across the Bay Area. Bay Area communities at risk of losing millions in homelessness funding Across the Bay Area, San Francisco, Alameda, and Santa Clara counties collectively receive more than $160 million in HUD funding each year to combat homelessness. Local officials, however, tell the NBC Bay Area Investigative Unit that between 40 and 65 percent of their funding could be cut because of the new restrictions on permanent housing programs. “Alameda County Health continues to be deeply concerned by HUD’s shift away from what we know works (i.e., permanent housing with individualized services to help people heal and stay housed),” Troy Espera, communications director for Alameda County Health, wrote in a statement. “This poses a challenge and local jurisdictions are struggling with the whiplash between HUD and legal actions.” Nationally, at least 97,000 people living in federally funded permanent housing could be at risk of losing their housing under the new rules, according to the National Alliance to End Homelessness, an advocacy group that joined Santa Clara County and eight other local governments and nonprofits in filing litigation against HUD to challenge the federal government’s new funding restrictions. Nonprofits, local governments sue HUD to halt its new funding rules Last month, those plaintiffs won a partial victory when a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to throw out its application process. The court found HUD failed to give the public required notice and an opportunity to comment on the changes before the new funding restrictions were implemented. Since the court determined HUD’s grant process was “procedurally invalid,” it declined to weigh in on the lawsuit’s other challenges, including the merits of HUD’s new funding restrictions. HUD later appealed and earlier this month a federal appeals court allowed HUD to restart the application process with the same funding changes while the court reviews the case. In granting the stay, the appeals court said HUD had made a “strong showing that it is likely to succeed” on the merits of its argument that the $1.3 billion in funding it set aside for transitional housing and other supportive services was not subject to that notice-and-comment requirement. The appeals court also determined further delays could create funding gaps for homelessness programs across the country. Opponents, including Santa Clara County, are still challenging HUD’s new policies in court, but the clock is ticking. Applications are now due to HUD by Wednesday at 5 p.m. PT. Congress requires HUD to award the funds by December 1. “I think there’s no doubt that there is a risk that the funding will not be issued when it’s supposed to be issued,” LoPresti said. “I think everybody’s concerned about that right now.” Contact The Investigative Unit submit tips | 1-888-996-TIPS | e-mail Bigad Follow @BigadShaban on social media Bigad Shaban

headlines.title: Watch: 1-on-1 interview with California governor candidate Steve Hilton
headlines.description: California will choose a new governor in November to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. Voters will decide between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years and also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. He recently joined NBC Bay Area for a wide-ranging discussion about his gubernatorial campaign, political philosophy and policy proposals. Watch the full one-on-one interview with Raj Mathai in the video above. Elections Sep 17 Elections Sep 14 Decision 2026 Jun 5 Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. NBC Bay Area reached out to Becerra multiple times for an interview and his campaign denied the requests. Since winning the primary, Becerra has kept a relatively low profile and has held a handful of public events, including an appearance in September at a rally in support of Proposition 1. Becerra did sit down for an interview with NBC Bay Area’s sister station, NBC Los Angeles, back in April. Watch the interview below.

headlines.title: Missing swimmer out of Antioch found dead
headlines.description: A swimmer who went missing last week in Antioch was discovered deceased, police said Tuesday. Edgielyn Torrente, 46, went missing while swimming near Smith’s Landing Seafood Grill on Wednesday. Torrente was found deceased in the San Joaquin River on Sunday. Just after 7 a.m. Sunday, officers responded to calls reporting a person in the water west of Smith’s Landing. The Contra Costa County Sheriff’s Office Marine Patrol and the Pittsburg Police Department recovered Torrente about a mile west of where she went missing. The Sheriff’s Office Coroner’s Division will determine the cause and manner of death. No foul play is suspected, according to police.

headlines.title: Pedestrian struck, killed by vehicle in SF's Richmond District
headlines.description: A pedestrian died after being struck by a motorist in San Francisco’s Richmond District on Monday afternoon, according to police. The collision was reported at 2:08 p.m. at the intersection of Arguello Boulevard and Anza Street. The pedestrian was taken to a hospital but died there, San Francisco police said. The driver of the vehicle involved in the collision stayed at the scene and cooperated with investigators, according to police. The name of the pedestrian was not immediately available.

headlines.title: OpenAI developer conference draws protests as company unveils new AI agents
headlines.description: Amid growing fears about the power of artificial intelligence and surrounded by protesters, OpenAI held its annual developer conference on Tuesday. The maker of ChatGPT also introduced new products during the event. Business and tech reporter Scott Budman reported that the focus of the day — and the reaction to it —depended on where you were standing. Inside the venue, the emphasis was on utilizing ChatGPT and other AI offerings rolled out by the company to make life easier. Outside, it was about demanding answers regarding safety concerns and fears that the city is turning into an AI-only enclave. As OpenAI CEO Sam Altman took the stage to cheers, a crowd outside San Francisco’s Fort Mason chanted his name in protest, shouting, “Sam Altman, get off it; choose people over profit.” Artificial intelligence Sep 26 Artificial intelligence Sep 22 Artificial intelligence Sep 17 Inside, the company showcased the latest version of its AI agents, called “Dots”. “This is the real-deal version of AI that we’ve always imagined for ourselves. It’s like an AI that always has your back, inspired by movies we all watched growing up,” presenters shared. The new agents can answer questions and execute tasks for users, acting as “a second set of eyes across everything I give it access to, and more importantly, a second set of hands to actually take work off my plate.” Outside, demonstrators focused on economic inequality and broader anxieties about what AI could do to humanity rather than for humanity. Many argued that the technology’s dominance in San Francisco is forcing long-term residents out. “We know that as soon as these IPOs happen, as soon as more money comes flowing into the city, we’re going to see a lot more evictions, and we need to be ready to scale up this fight,” said Molly Goldberg of the SF Anti-Displacement Coalition. It is a conflict over both money and safety tied to what all sides believe could be transformational technology.

headlines.title: 2 killed, 3 injured in multi-vehicle crash in East Palo Alto
headlines.description: Two people were killed and at least three others were injured in a seven-vehicle crash in East Palo Alto Tuesday morning, according to the San Mateo County Sheriff’s Office. The crash happened at about 8:20 a.m. in the area of Bay Road and University Avenue. Investigators said a minivan struck six other vehicles, including a SamTrans Ride Plus van, before coming to rest on Bay Road. The driver of the minivan, an adult man, suffered serious injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene. An adult woman who was also in the minivan was taken to a hospital with life-threatening injuries, where she later died. At least three other people were injured in the crash. None of those injuries were reported as life-threatening, according to the sheriff’s office. The cause of the crash is under investigation. Anyone who witnessed the crash or has additional information is asked to contact the San Mateo County Sheriff’s Office at 650-363-4911.

headlines.title: San Jose leaders to vote on parking meter rate increase
headlines.description: The cost to park in downtown San Jose could soon be going up. The San Jose City Council on Tuesday is scheduled to vote on a plan to double the downtown parking meter rate to $4 per hour and extend parking meter hours to 9 p.m. instead of the current end time of 6 p.m. One member of the city’s Downtown Parking Board sent an open letter to the council recommending it postpone the vote. Tuesday’s meeting starts at 1:30 p.m.

headlines.title: New California law bans officers from using gloves that deliver electric shocks
headlines.description: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law Tuesday banning local, state and federal law enforcement officers from using gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to people. The ban on shock gloves will take effect next year and remain in place until 2030. It comes weeks after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement moved to equip its officers with the gloves, which are designed to gain compliance from combative individuals. Last month, the agency awarded a nearly $17 million contract to buy 6,000 pairs. “Trump has put his political interests above the health, safety and livelihood of American families,” Newsom said in a statement. “California is taking action to strengthen transparency, accountability, and oversight around immigration enforcement in our state.” The law is the latest example of how Democratic-led states have been pushing back against President Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts since he took office last year. In California, lawmakers passed at least two dozen bills this year seeking to fortify immigrants’ rights, restrict cooperation with federal immigration agents and tighten regulations on immigrant detention facilities, among other things. Newsom signed many of them Tuesday. Nationwide, 17 states with Democratic-led legislatures have passed a total of more than 100 pro-immigrant bills this year, according to an Associated Press analysis using the bill tracking software Plural. The most common purpose is to limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement agents. Democratic California Assemblymember LaShae Sharp-Collins said she introduced the shock-gloves legislation to “put a pause” on law enforcement’s use of the devices while the state examines their potential risks. The law requires the state’s Justice Department to study their safety and report to lawmakers by 2029. “There’s a lot of unrest and a lot of uncertainty,” she said in an interview. “A lot of people are scared.” The law will again test the state’s authority to restrict federal agents amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. A federal judge earlier this year blocked the state’s first-in-the-nation law barring federal officers from wearing face coverings, deeming it too selective because it applied to local and federal law enforcement but exempted state officers. Lawmakers passed a new bill this year to make the ban apply to all officers. Newsom signed that legislation. Kevin Johnson, a professor emeritus at the University of California, Davis, School of Law, said courts ultimately are likely to rule that the state cannot bar federal officers from wearing shock gloves or face coverings. The laws are well-intentioned, he said, but likely conflict with the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution, which generally sets federal law as supreme over conflicting state law. “The state has very limited, if any, powers in dictating to the federal government how its officers are armed,” he said. California law enforcement groups broadly opposed the ban, and First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, a Trump appointee, said the state didn’t have the authority to limit which weapons federal officers use. “Governor, we’ve been through this already,” he wrote on X. “If you want to regulate federal agents, you have to win a federal election. Until then, you have no jurisdiction.” Essayli also suggested federal officers would defy a law Newsom signed restricting them from using flash-bang grenades during protests and immigration enforcement. “Or what? You’re going to write us a ticket,” Essayli posted. Sacramento Sheriff Jim Cooper, a Democrat and former state lawmaker, said banning shock gloves “really makes no sense” because they are among the nonlethal tools officers can use if necessary. “When the federal government does something, the state Legislature wants to ban it,” he said at a news conference. “They’re making our job harder.” Sharp-Collins said ICE’s plan to use shock gloves was the catalyst for the ban. But she cited their use by other officers, including a case in which a Kentucky family alleges a man died after being tased and shocked with the gloves dozens of times while in law enforcement custody in 2024. State Sen. Scott Wiener, a San Francisco Democrat who wrote last year’s mask ban, also authored this year’s measure to expand it to state officers. “California must use every available tool to stand up for our communities under attack from ICE’s secret police terror campaign,” he said in a statement after it passed the Legislature. ___ Associated Press writer David A. Lieb contributed to this report from Jefferson City, Missouri.

headlines.title: San Francisco to keep Flock cameras with new limits on data access
headlines.description: San Francisco will keep its Flock license plate cameras but put new limits on who can access the data they record, officials announced Tuesday. City leaders said they want to strike a balance between effective law enforcement and protecting civil liberties. Under the new policy, officers will need approval from leadership and a connection to an active criminal investigation to search data tied to the city’s network of automated license plate readers (ALPR). The data will also be removed from Flock’s platform after 30 days. San Francisco police will keep their own copy for up to a year. The city’s Department of Police Accountability will also conduct regular audits on how the department is handing its ALPR data. The city’s Human Rights Commission recently completed its own independent audit, making a few recommendations on better practices. The police department has also conducted its own internal audits and announced some of its key findings earlier this year that led to tightened controls on outside agencies that access the city’s ALPR data. District Attorney Brooke Jenkins said she asked state Assemblymember Matt Haney to work on state legislation that would make it a crime for a police officer or anyone else to access ALPR data for personal or inappropriate reasons. “I became concerned not only with the fact that people were being put in harm’s way by the misuse and abuse of access to this data, but also that if that continued to happen we would compromise our ability here in San Francisco to be able to continue to use the technology,” Jenkins said. Jenkins and Haney are considering if proposed state legal sanctions would be misdemeanor and/or potentially felony charges.

headlines.title: Preliminary 2.6 magnitude earthquake strikes near Yountville
headlines.description: A preliminary 2.6 magnitude earthquake struck near Yountville Tuesday morning, according to the United States Geological Survey. The quake hit at 9:06 a.m. and was centered 2.9 miles south-southwest of Oakville, 7.6 miles north-northeast of Sonoma and 10.3 miles northwest of Napa, the USGS said. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. headlines.title: Bicyclist, electric scooter rider injured in separate San Jose collisions
headlines.description: A bicyclist and an electric scooter rider were injured Monday in separate collisions in San Jose, according to police. The first collision happened at about 3:05 p.m. near the intersection of South Seventh and East Virginia streets, police said. A bicyclist was taken to a local hospital to be treated for non-life-threatening injuries, according to police. The driver stayed at the scene and cooperated with investigators. The second collision happened at roughly 6:09 p.m. in the area of McKee Road and Interstate 680, police said. A man riding an electric scooter was taken to local hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, according to police. The driver remained at the scene and was cooperative with the investigation. Alcohol and/or drugs do not appear to have played a role in either collision, police said. Both collisions are under investigation.
